title: Build a new component, from its ticket to the Bank's repository
summary: New code written to the firm's rules from its first line: built, documented, tested and improved, audited, and committed with its evidence
story: Disputes Operations keep card payment disputes in a spreadsheet, so reconciliation cannot see which settled payments are disputed. Priya Nair builds dispute intake into the settlement service with NexCODE: the code and its tests, its documentation to the Bank's standard, improvements with the tests run before and after, a security audit against the Bank's standards and OWASP, and a commit to the Bank's repository with the evidence record beside the code.

card.about: New code is where a bank's rules matter most and are easiest to miss. NexCODE builds a new component of the settlement service from its ticket, to the four layers of rules from the first line: card numbers masked, money in Decimal, bound SQL parameters and an audit event. It documents the module to the Code Documentation Standard, with a tool showing no line of code changed; reads the test results and recommends improvements, then makes them with their tests; audits the code against the Bank's standards and OWASP ASVS, each finding traced to the regulation; and commits the code with its evidence record to the Bank's repository for review.
card.scenario: Monday 10 August 2026. Hannah Clarke of Disputes Operations raised DSP-2026-03 on 3 August: card payment disputes are kept in a spreadsheet, and the scheme's deadlines are tracked by hand. Priya Nair builds dispute intake in the settlement service, Python like the rest of the service, from the ticket to a branch in the Bank's repository.

steps.title: Build it
steps.prompt: Build dispute intake for ticket DSP-2026-03 in the settlement service, in Python 3.13, the service's language. Write nexus-payments/services/settlement/dispute_intake.py with record_dispute(conn, transaction_id, card_number, amount, reason_code, received_on, actor): look up the card transaction by its id; refuse a dispute for an unknown transaction, for one that is not CAPTURED, or for an amount that is not positive or is more than the transaction's amount; store the dispute in a disputes table (create it if it is missing) with the card number masked to its last four digits, the amount, the reason code, the date and the status OPEN; emit an audit event for it; and return the stored dispute. Write nexus-payments/services/settlement/test_dispute_intake.py with unit tests (unittest, an in-memory SQLite database loaded from fixtures/settlement_fixture.sql) for an accepted dispute and for each refusal.

talkTrack: New code is where the rules matter most. Select the demo: the ticket and the service's existing module open; there is nothing to fix, something to build. Build it: NexCODE explains the design in plain words, citing the rules from all four layers, and the module and its tests open in the IDE as new files; Apply, run the tests. Comment it: NexCODE writes the header from the team's template, with the Bank's notices and the AI disclosure, and a docstring for every function; the checks run the tests again and a tool that reads the Python itself shows no line of code changed. Test and improve: NexCODE reads the test results with the code and recommends improvements, each with its reason and rule, then makes them with their tests; the tests run again, before and after in the record. Security audit: the pre-merge checks run first, then NexCODE's own findings against the Bank's standards and OWASP ASVS, each traced to the regulation's text; a blocking finding gets its fix. Record the change, then Commit: the module, its tests and the evidence record go on feature/DSP-2026-03 in the Bank's repository, labelled AI-assisted, for David Vance to review. Point at the card: SVS-020 keeps the evidence with the change.
